title: Do the two diagonal sums match in every square of four dates?
description: A square of four dates is marked on the November calendar, and the two dates on each diagonal are added. Calling the top left date a, the other three dates are written with a, and both diagonal sums come out the same. Keeko's doubt is that the sums are equal only for the marked square.
teaching_notes: One idea: a letter-number for the top left date lets one working cover every square of the calendar. Watch for students who think the letter stands for one fixed date.

source: In the calendar square with 12, 13 on the top and 19, 20 bel
video_script.why: A learner sees how a letter for the top left date shows that both diagonal sums are equal in every square.
video_script.substitution: the book's marked square of the November calendar, with the top left date called a
video_script.anchor: the calendar of November with the marked square of four dates, twelve and thirteen on the top, nineteen and twenty below
video_script.wrong_answer: the two sums are equal only for the marked square
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko thinks the letter stands for one fixed date, so the result holds for the marked square alone. A square with top left date twenty gives forty eight on both diagonals, so the same steps hold for every square.
video_script.payoff_line: Both diagonal sums are two eigh plus eight

final_answer.value: 2a + 8 ; both sums are 32 for the marked square
final_answer.spoken: both diagonal sums are two eigh plus eight, and thirty two for the marked square

maths_rules: the date to the right of a is a + 1, the date below is a + 7 (a week has 7 days), the diagonal date is a + 8
Keeko test, top left 20: 20 + 28 = 48 and 21 + 27 = 48 and 2 x 20 + 8 = 40 + 8 = 48
video_script.design: The calendar square stays on the board. The four dates are renamed with a, the two diagonals are added one under the other, and the result is checked on the marked square.

narration: <bookmark mark='scene'/>This is a question from your book about the calendar of November two thousand twenty four.
<bookmark mark='sq'/>The book marks a small square of four dates. Twelve and thirteen are on the top, and nineteen and twenty are below.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Add the two dates joined by each slanting line. Will the two sums be equal in every such square?

beats.on_screen: the calendar and the marked square stay on the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: the square with its two slanting lines labelled diagonal; the dates 12 and 19 joined by an arrow marked 7 more

marks.diag: the two slanting lines are labelled diagonal
marks.week: an arrow from 12 down to 19 is marked seven more
marks.next: an arrow from 12 across to 13 is marked one more

narration: <bookmark mark='diag'/>A slanting line across the square is called a diagonal.
<bookmark mark='week'/>A week has seven days, so the date directly below a date is seven more.
<bookmark mark='next'/>The date to the right is one more.

beats.on_screen: Given: a square of four dates, 12 and 13 on the top, 19 and 20 below

marks.gv: the four dates are written as a small square

narration: <bookmark mark='gv'/>Given, a square of four dates from the calendar. Twelve and thirteen are on the top, and nineteen and twenty are below.

beats.on_screen: To find: the sum on each diagonal, and whether the two sums are equal for every square

marks.fd: the aim is written under the given

narration: <bookmark mark='fd'/>We have to add the dates on each diagonal. Then we show that the two sums are equal for every square of four dates.
<bookmark mark='first'/>Step one, add the dates on each diagonal of the marked square.
<bookmark mark='second'/>Twelve plus twenty is thirty two, and thirteen plus nineteen is thirty two.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: top left = a ; right = a + 1 ; below = a + 7 ; diagonal = a + 8

marks.name: the letter a is written on the top left date
marks.right: a + 1 is written on the right
marks.diag: a + 8 is written on the diagonal date

narration: <bookmark mark='name'/>Step two, call the top left date eigh, because it can be any date.
<bookmark mark='right'/>The date to its right is one more, so it is eigh plus one.
<bookmark mark='below'/>The date below is seven more, so it is eigh plus seven.
<bookmark mark='diag'/>The date on the diagonal is one more and seven more, so it is eigh plus eight.

marks.d1: the first diagonal is added and its bracket is opened
marks.d2: the second diagonal is added and its brackets are opened
marks.d2r: a + a and 1 + 7 are grouped to give 2a + 8

narration: <bookmark mark='d1'/>Step three, add the first diagonal, eigh and eigh plus eight. Terms can be added in any order, so the bracket can be opened.
<bookmark mark='d1r'/>Eigh plus eigh plus eight is two eigh plus eight.
<bookmark mark='d2'/>The other diagonal is eigh plus one and eigh plus seven.
<bookmark mark='d2r'/>Opening the brackets, eigh and eigh make two eigh, and one and seven make eight. This is also two eigh plus eight.

beats.on_screen: Step 4, check with a = 12: 2 × 12 + 8 = 24 + 8 = 32, the same as 32 and 32

marks.chkv: 2 × 12 + 8 is worked out and matched with 32

narration: <bookmark mark='chk'/>Step four, check with the marked square, where eigh is twelve.
<bookmark mark='chkv'/>Two times twelve plus eight is twenty four plus eight, which is thirty two. It matches both sums.

beats.on_screen: Answer: 2a + 8 ; for the marked square both sums are 32
narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Both diagonal sums are two eigh plus eight, so they are equal in every square. For the marked square, both are thirty two.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the calendar square
narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's bubble: equal only for the marked square, struck out; a new square 20, 21 over 27, 28 with both diagonals 48

marks.try: a new square with top left 20 appears
marks.fix: the bubble is struck out and 2 × 20 + 8 = 48 is written

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks the two sums are equal only for the marked square.
<bookmark mark='try'/>Try another square, with the top left date as twenty. The dates are twenty, twenty one, twenty seven and twenty eight.
<bookmark mark='sums'/>Twenty plus twenty eight is forty eight, and twenty one plus twenty seven is forty eight.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>Two times twenty plus eight is forty eight too. Eigh can be any top left date, so the same steps hold for every square.
